title: Language constructs
lede: The core TypeScript surface this compiler lowers to native code: control flow, operators, declarations, functions and closures, async/Promise, and classes. Most of it matches JS/TS exactly, but the recurring divergences are worth knowing up front — strings are NUL-terminated (an embedded null truncates), a nullable scalar's null is often an in-band presence bit rather than a real undefined, `-compat` governs whether `&&`/`||` are value-preserving, and a top-level `const`/`let` is only readable from a named function when its type is knowable before main() runs (an arrow closure captures anything regardless). The whole surface is statically typed and structurally shaped — there is no dynamic property add/delete and no runtime eval.

entries.name: if / else if / else
entries.description: Conditional branching with the usual else-if chain and optional braceless single-statement bodies.

entries.name: while loop
entries.description: Pre-condition loop; the body runs zero or more times.

entries.name: do…while loop
entries.description: Post-condition loop; the body always runs at least once before the condition is checked. break/continue work inside it.

entries.name: for (init; cond; update)
entries.description: The C-style three-clause for loop.

entries.name: for…of over arrays, strings, Map, Set, and a class implementing next(): T | null
entries.statusRow: for…of over arrays, strings, Map, Set, and a class implementing next(): T | null
entries.description: Iterates arrays, a string (its characters), Map (values), Set (elements), generators, and both the structural next(): T | null shape and the spec's real [Symbol.iterator]() protocol. The loop variable may be a destructuring pattern, including nested. A scalar next() returns a presence-flagged aggregate so a yielded 0/false doesn't end iteration.
differences: A bare `for (const v of map)` iterates values (use `.keys()` for keys); the two-name pattern `for (const [k, v] of map)` decomposes entries.
A string iterates per byte, not per Unicode code point — correct for ASCII/Latin-1.

entries.name: for…in over object keys
entries.description: Iterates the field names of an object as strings.

entries.name: switch / case / default / break
entries.description: Multi-way branch with numeric, string, and boolean discriminants.

entries.name: break / continue in loops, including labeled (outer: for (...) { break outer; })
entries.statusRow: break / continue in loops, including labeled (outer: for (...) { break outer; })
entries.description: Loop break/continue, including a labeled target on an enclosing loop. A break/continue inside a nested closure can only target a loop declared within that closure's own body — a clean compile-time rejection otherwise, matching JS's no-cross-function-boundary label rule.

entries.name: return
entries.description: Typed return; an implicit void return is handled.

entries.name: throw new Error(msg)
entries.description: Throws via setjmp/longjmp. A built-in error constructor is also a first-class value (a boxed funcref with exact identity, typeof "function").

entries.name: try / catch / finally
entries.description: Exception handling with a single catch variable or a destructured object pattern. finally runs on early return/break/continue (labeled or not), a return in finally overrides, and nested finallys run innermost-first — inside async functions and generators too, including a finally that itself awaits.
differences: A catch pattern can only destructure the caught value's fixed `{kind, message, name}` shape (every thrown value, including a thrown non-Error primitive, is force-shaped into that one runtime layout), not an arbitrary custom object's own fields, and there's no array-pattern form.

entries.name: Optional catch binding (try {} catch {}, no bound param)
entries.statusRow: Optional catch binding (try {} catch {}, no bound param) — ES2019
entries.description: The catch parameter clause is optional (ES2019).

entries.name: debugger statement
entries.description: Parsed and erased to a no-op — an AOT-compiled native binary has no attached inspector to break into, matching plain JS with no debugger attached. debugger is a reserved word, never a real identifier.

entries.name: Numeric literals (42, 3.14, 0xFF, 0b101, 0o77)
entries.description: Decimal, float, hex, binary, and octal numeric literals.

entries.name: Numeric separators (1_000_000)
entries.description: Underscore digit separators, stripped at lex time so every downstream consumer sees a clean literal. A leading/trailing/doubled separator, or one inside a legacy-octal literal, is a clean lexer error.

entries.name: String literals (single/double quote)
entries.description: Single- and double-quoted strings; the full ES escape grammar is decoded (\b \f \v, \xHH, \uHHHH, \u{H…}, Annex B legacy octal, line continuation, and the NonEscapeCharacter rule). Templates share the same decoding.
differences: An embedded NUL (`\x00`, `\0`) truncates the string, since strings are stored as NUL-terminated C strings.
No strict-mode `SyntaxError` for a legacy octal escape (accepted unconditionally).

entries.name: Boolean literals (true / false)
entries.description: Boolean literals.

entries.name: null literal
entries.description: The null literal; a T | null union type is supported.

entries.name: undefined literal
entries.description: The undefined literal.

entries.name: Template literals `Hello ${name}`
entries.description: Backtick template literals with arbitrary interpolation depth.

entries.name: Arithmetic operators + - * / %
entries.signature: a + b - c * d / e % f
entries.description: The five basic arithmetic operators.

entries.name: ** (exponentiation)
entries.description: Right-associative exponentiation (ES2016), binding tighter than * / %, with **=. number operands are doubles so 2 ** -1 is 0.5 and 2 ** 0.5 is a real root; explicit integer-typed operands use exact i64 exponentiation-by-squaring and stay i64. -2 ** 2 is a SyntaxError, matching JS.

entries.name: Comparison operators == === != !== < > <= >=
entries.description: The comparison operators; string comparison via strcmp. NaN compares per JS: NaN !== NaN is true while ===/</>/<=/>= against NaN are all false.

entries.name: Logical operators && || !
entries.description: Genuinely short-circuiting logical operators. Result type is bool under -compat=strict (default); -compat=js makes &&/|| value-preserving for same-typed operands (x || "default" yields the string).
differences: Under `-compat=js`, `&&`/`||` are value-preserving only for **same-typed** operands; differently-typed operands (`0 || "x"`) stay bool, since the value-preserving result would be a union this compiler can't represent.

entries.name: Bitwise operators & | ^ ~ << >> >>>
entries.signature: a & b, a << b, a >>> b
entries.description: The bitwise and shift operators, including the unsigned right shift >>>.

entries.name: Assignment operators += -= *= /= %= &= |= ^= <<= >>= >>>=
entries.description: The full set of compound assignment operators.

entries.name: Logical assignment operators &&= ||= ??=
entries.description: Genuinely short-circuiting logical assignment (ES2021). Works against scalar variables, array elements, object fields, static class fields, and a computed dynamic-object key (dynObj[key] ??= v), including a nullable-scalar field routed through the presence-flagged path so obj.n ??= v fires exactly when the field is absent.

entries.name: Increment / decrement ++ -- (prefix & postfix)
entries.description: Prefix and postfix increment/decrement on an identifier, member (obj.x++, this.x++, C.staticField++, makeObj().x++), or index (arr[i]++, makeArr()[i]++) target. A member/index target desugars to += 1 / -= 1; prefix yields the new value, postfix the old. A consumed postfix hoists any side-effecting component so each runs exactly once, matching JS.

entries.name: Ternary cond ? a : b
entries.description: The conditional (ternary) operator.

entries.name: Comma / sequence operator (a, b, c)
entries.description: Evaluates each operand left to right and yields the last (its type is the sequence's type). Also usable in a for header.
differences: A sequence whose *first* operand is a lone identifier (`(a, b)`) is instead parsed as an arrow-function parameter list — a known ambiguity; write a non-identifier first operand.

entries.name: Nullish coalescing ??
entries.description: Works on a pointer T | null (string/object/…) and a non-pointer scalar T | null (number | null, boolean | null) via a real presence bit — so let x: number | null = null; x ?? 42 yields 42 while a present 0 yields 0.

entries.name: Optional chaining ?.
entries.description: Null-guards pointer fields; returns null on a null receiver.

entries.name: typeof operator
entries.description: Compile-time constant resolved from inferred type. Heap-backed built-in values (a Promise, Map/Set, a generator, Date, null) are "object"; classes, implemented built-in constructors, and implemented global functions are "function"; Math/JSON/console are "object"; an undeclared name or runtime-absent static is "undefined".
differences: `typeof <namespace>.<method>` answers `"function"` for the common built-in namespaces (`Promise`/`Math`/`JSON`, `console`, and the static methods of `Object`/`Number`/`String`/`Array`/`Date`/`Symbol`/`Reflect`); a non-method static (`Number.MAX_VALUE`) answers through normal inference, and a namespace outside this allow-list falls back to inference.

`typeof value.method` is `"function"` for a class instance method or a common built-in string/array method (a class getter reads as its return type); a string/array method name outside the curated set falls back to inference.

entries.name: in operator (key in obj)
entries.description: Reduces to the same compile-time FieldIndex lookup Object.hasOwn() uses — object shapes are fully structural/static, so a string-literal key against an object is a compile-time-constant true/false, not a runtime scan. Parsed as a contextual keyword at instanceof precedence.

entries.name: Spread in array literals [...a, ...b]
entries.description: Array-literal spread.

entries.name: const / let / var declarations
entries.signature: const x = 1; let y; var z;
entries.description: var is function-scoped and re-declarable; let/const are block-scoped and const rebinding is rejected. A top-level const/let/var is a module global — readable and writable from any named function whenever its type is determinable before main() runs. Block redeclaration, TDZ, and use-before-assignment are compile errors.
differences: Definite-assignment analysis is sound-not-complete: a typed `var`/`let` assigned only in a maybe-skipped loop or across correlated conditions still falls through to the `undefined`/zero default rather than raising `used before being assigned`.

A top-level `const`/`let` still isn't readable from a named `function` only in the invariant's genuine edges — a `bigint`, a *scalar*-returning un-annotated call (the `i64` default), a `new Set([…])` typed from its initializer array, or an init depending on a runtime-local (a `{ …rest }` spread of a destructuring target); an arrow/closure still captures any of them.

entries.name: Array destructuring const [a, b] = arr
entries.description: Array destructuring with holes, defaults (fire when past the source length), and a rest element that makes a real independent copy. Usable as a for-of loop variable and a destructured parameter; nested patterns work in a declaration/for-of/parameter.
differences: *Assignment* to already-declared targets (`[a, b] = expr`, not a fresh declaration) reaches declaration-form parity for nesting: nested array/object patterns, a trailing `...rest`, and a per-element `= default` all work. A compound operator (`[a, b] += …`) and a member target (`[obj.x] = e`) stay rejected.

entries.name: Object destructuring const { x, y } = obj
entries.statusRow: Object destructuring const { x, y } = obj
entries.description: Object destructuring with renaming, string/numeric-literal keys, nested patterns, and a rest element that binds a fresh residual object. Usable as a for-of loop variable and destructured parameter. Assignment to already-declared targets requires parens.
differences: Default values (`{ x = 1 }`) are supported only for a field typed as a nullable *reference* (`T | null` where T is string/array/object/class) — the only field shape with a real "not provided" signal; a default on a nullable scalar or any non-nullable field is a clean compile-time rejection.

*Assignment* to already-declared targets supports nested patterns (`({ p, q: { r } } = obj)`, `({ arr: [x, y] } = obj)`) and object-property defaults (`{ x = default }`, `{ k: x = default }`) on a nullable-reference field, at declaration-form parity.
`{ ...rest }` over an `any`/union/generic source and in the *assignment* form (`({ a, ...rest } = e)`) stay clean rejections.
A computed key (`{ [k]: v }`) is supported only for a constant string/number literal key (`{ ["a"]: v }`, `{ [0]: v }`); a runtime-valued key on a fixed object is a clean rejection.

entries.name: Tagged template literals
entries.description: Desugars to a plain call (tag(["a","b"], x)) — interpolated values reach the tag as real typed values, not implicitly stringified. Any callable works as a tag, including an arrow/closure with a ...rest parameter.
differences: A user tag's `strings` argument has no `.raw` property (arrays carry no extra properties); the built-in `String.raw` tag itself is implemented and interleaves the raw, un-escaped quasis.

entries.name: Function declarations (top-level)
entries.description: Named top-level functions with typed params and return. A leading this parameter (function f(this: T, …)) is parsed and erased, exactly as real TS does. The synthesized arguments object supports .length, indexing, and for…of when all declared params share one type.
differences: Cannot reference a sibling top-level binding whose value is a connection handle (`Worker`/`WebSocket`/`EventSource`, `BroadcastChannel`/`MessageChannel`, `XMLHttpRequest`), a `Promise`, or a generic class instance with **inferred** rather than explicit type arguments (`new Box(5)`) — such a binding stays a `main()` local and fails with `undefined variable`. Scalars, strings, arrays, `TypedArray`s, objects, `Map`/`Set`, class instances (including explicit `new Box<number>()`), the value/event handles, and the streams + `EventEmitter` and `http.createServer` handles are promoted to module globals; arrow functions/closures capture everything regardless.
A genuinely circular pair of mutually-recursive unannotated functions can't converge on a return type and keeps the scalar-default fallback.

The `arguments` object reflects the declared parameters rather than growing with extra untyped arguments; mixed-type parameters, a rest/destructured parameter, and an arrow function (which has no own `arguments` in JS) are clean rejections.

entries.name: Arrow functions / lambdas
entries.description: Full closures; captures via a heap-allocated env struct.

entries.name: Function expressions
entries.statusRow: Function expressions (var f = function(x) {...}, callback arguments, IIFE bodies)
entries.description: Anonymous and named function expressions, including as callback arguments. A named function expression binds its own name inside its own body for recursion without leaking — even when that name shadows a top-level function of the same name (the self-reference is the expression; outer calls reach the top-level function). async function(...) {...} expressions are supported. Reuses arrow closure machinery.
differences: A generic function used by value is out of scope (no single monomorphized symbol to point at).

entries.name: Default parameter values
entries.description: Default parameter values.
differences: A default may reference an earlier scalar/string parameter — `function f(a: number, b: number = a * 2)`, chaining included (`c = b + 1`) — for a free function, an instance/static method, and a constructor (parameter properties included, `constructor(public x = 1, public y = x)`); an earlier param of any supported kind is referenceable — scalar/string, array (`b = a.length`, `a[i]`), and nullable-scalar (`b = (a ?? 0) + 1`). A rest-parameter constructor is unsupported.

entries.name: Optional parameters (param?)
entries.description: Optional parameters.
differences: An omitted `?` argument gets the parameter type's zero value — the same `undefined` stand-in default parameter values/destructuring defaults use, not real JS's `undefined`.

entries.name: Rest parameters (...args: number[])
entries.description: Works on named function declarations, class methods, arrow functions/closures, and function type annotations ((...xs: number[]) => R and the same as a type alias) alike.

entries.name: Destructured function parameters
entries.statusRow: Destructured function parameters (function f({ x, y }: T) {} / function f([a, b]: T[]) {})
entries.description: Object- and array-destructured parameters. Each element/field may have its own default; nested patterns work; supported on named functions, class methods/constructors, and arrow functions.
differences: Requires an explicit type annotation on the pattern (no sensible unannotated default the way a scalar param has); no combination with `...` or a whole-parameter default value.
A `= default` on a nested position is a clean rejection; per-element defaults follow the same rules as the statement-level destructuring rows.

entries.name: Nested function declarations
entries.statusRow: Nested function declarations (function outer() { function inner() {...}; return inner(); })
entries.description: A helper function declared inside another function's body — hoisted, forward-referenceable, self-recursive, and visible to its own further-nested descendants.
differences: A declaration inside a lexical block (an `if`/`for`/`while`/`do-while`/bare block, `try`/`catch`/`finally`, or a `switch` case) is supported and block-scoped; the residual is the specialized `for…of`/`for…in` iterator variants (generator/stream/`Symbol.iterator` paths) that iterate their body directly (no miscompile — capturing such a loop variable is a clean rejection).
A block-nested declaration capturing a C-style `for` loop variable is a clean rejection — the loop variable is a single per-iteration cell; copy it to a `const` inside the loop body and capture that.

Captures enclosing locals/parameters by reference, but only for use **at or after** the declaration point — a capturing nested function called before its declaration is a clean error (a non-capturing one keeps full hoisting/forward-reference). Capturing an array variable, and a capturing nested *generator*, stay clean rejections.
Generic (`<T>`) nested declarations and same-scope duplicate names are clean compile errors.

entries.name: Function.prototype.call / .apply / .bind
entries.signature: f.call(thisArg, a, b); f.apply(null, arr); f.bind(null, a)
entries.description: f.call/f.apply lower to a direct call; f.apply(thisArg, arr) spreads into a rest slot; f.bind builds a new partially-applied closure. All type-checked against f's parameters exactly as a normal call.
differences: `thisArg` is evaluated then **ignored** — a closure has no rebindable `this`, so method-borrowing is unsupported; only the arguments are forwarded.
Only on a first-class function **value** (a closure, function parameter, arrow/function expression, or named function) — call/apply/bind on a built-in isn't supported.
`.apply` takes either a literal array or a runtime array spread into a **rest** parameter; a runtime array into a fixed-arity function is the usual spread-into-fixed-arity rejection.
`.bind` is V1-scoped to functions whose parameters are plain scalar/string/pointer types with no rest slot — an array/nullable-scalar/rest parameter is a clean compile error.

entries.name: Function overload signatures
entries.statusRow: Function overload signatures (function f(x: number): number; + impl)
entries.description: Overload signature heads (a `function` head terminated by `;` with no body) are parsed and then erased — call sites type-check against the implementation's parameter list, matching this compiler's TS-modifier stance.
differences: Overload heads are **erased**, not used for per-signature overload resolution: a call is checked against the implementation signature only, so give it parameter/return types (often a union) wide enough to cover every overload.

entries.name: Generator functions
entries.statusRow: Generator functions (function* f(): T { yield x; }, .next(value), for...of)
entries.description: Real suspend/resume via this compiler's ucontext-based fiber primitive. The full iterator protocol: .throw(e) injects at the suspension point, .return(v) completes running enclosing finally blocks, and yield* delegates to an inner generator.
differences: A free `function*` may be top-level **or nested** (a nested one captures enclosing state by reference; an *array* capture stays a clean rejection); a generator *expression* is supported only as a top-level `const/let/var G = function* ...` binding — an argument/nested/IIFE use is a clean rejection. `static`/`abstract` generator methods stay clean rejections.
The return-type annotation is optional (inferred from the body's yields); still requires a plain non-destructured parameter list and a non-array element/parameter type.
Calling `.next()` again after completion returns `{value: <T's zero value>, done: true}` — this compiler's usual stand-in for real JS's `undefined`.

entries.name: async functions
entries.description: Every async fn returns a real task-shaped Promise<T>: a fn containing an await runs on a ucontext fiber; a no-await one settles inline. Named declarations, async arrows, and async function expressions are all supported. No libcurl linked unless fetch is used.

entries.name: await expressions
entries.description: A Promise is a reusable value — await p twice returns the same result. Every await yields a microtask tick, of an already-settled promise and of a non-promise value, FIFO-ordered with .then/queueMicrotask, matching JS. Registers a resume reaction and parks.

entries.name: Promise.all / .race / .allSettled
entries.description: Real concurrency over Array<Promise<Response>> (fetch) and over Array<Promise<T>> from may-suspend async fns. Each member is a reusable value. .race/.any return the shortest-delay member via an event-driven waiter list. A rejecting member rejects .all/.race and reports rejected in .allSettled.

entries.name: Promise.any
entries.description: Over task promises it skips rejected members and resolves to the first fulfilled one; when every member rejects it throws a real AggregateError carrying each reason on .errors. Over raw fetches, an HTTP 404/500 is a fulfilled fetch, per WHATWG.

entries.name: Promise.resolve / Promise.reject
entries.description: Both build a settled task promise, so await/.then/.catch/.finally and the combinators all work. Promise.resolve(v) fulfils with v (an already-promise arg flattens through); Promise.reject(e) is typed Promise<never>, so a rejected value assigns to any binding. No fiber/libcurl linked.

entries.name: new Promise((resolve, reject) => …)
entries.description: The executor constructor with thenable adoption (resolve(anotherPromise) settles the outer promise with the inner's value, reaction-based), synchronous resolve/reject, first-settle-wins, and deferred resolution from a setTimeout callback. The executor may be an arrow, function expression, closure variable, or bare top-level-function reference.
differences: Only a typed `Promise` argument adopts; a custom duck-typed `{ then }` object isn't adopted (this compiler has no `PromiseLike<T>` type — it's a clean type mismatch, not a silent miss).

entries.name: Promise.prototype.then / .catch / .finally + queueMicrotask
entries.description: .then/.catch/.finally directly on a raw fetch Promise<Response> never block the synchronous script — the wait is deferred to a queued microtask. The callback runs as a microtask when the promise settles and its result chains into the returned promise. A missing callback slot is a pass-through. queueMicrotask is a FIFO drained after the sync script and before timers.

entries.name: Async generators (async function*, async *m())
entries.signature: async function* f() { yield await x; }
entries.description: V8/spec step timing: .next() starts the body synchronously up to the first await/yield; an await inside the body parks the step. Top-level or nested async function* and a class async *m() method. .next() returns a real Promise<{value,done}>. Full protocol: .throw(e)/.return(v) and yield* over an inner async generator or a Symbol.asyncIterator iterable.

entries.name: for await...of (async iteration)
entries.description: Consumes an async-generator instance, a user class or object literal implementing the async-iteration protocol, or any sync iterable the sync for...of takes (awaiting each element). Awaits each .next() promise before reading .done/.value; the loop is itself a suspension point. A destructuring loop variable unpacks each element.

entries.name: Enums (numeric)
entries.description: Numeric enums with auto-increment and explicit values.
entries.snippet:
enum Direction {
  North,
  East,
  South,
  West,
}
console.log(Direction.East)  // 1

entries.name: Enums (string)
entries.description: String enums; members are interned string constants. The enum name (and its [] array form) as a type annotation resolves to the enum's ptr backing type, so a typed variable/param/field/array, comparison, and switch all work.

entries.name: Namespaces (namespace X {}, function merging)
entries.description: Merges with a same-name top-level function X(...) — TS's callable-object duality idiom (assert(x) + assert.sameValue(...)); members desugar to flat top-level declarations.
differences: V1 scope: top-level only, members must be `export function` / `export const`/`let` (single binding); no nesting, no `declare namespace`, no cross-module `export namespace`; the same namespace member declared in two files is a link-time duplicate-symbol error, not file-private.

entries.name: Interfaces (structural)
entries.description: Structural interfaces backed by heap-allocated objects.

entries.name: Type aliases
entries.description: Type alias declarations.

entries.name: Object literals { key: value }
entries.description: A key may be an identifier, or a string/numeric literal.
differences: Constant-key bracket access reads and writes the matching field on a fixed object or class instance (`o["a"]`, `o[0]`, `o["a"] = v`) — the same field `o.a` reaches; a non-constant key on a fixed object stays a clean rejection (use a `{ [k: string]: T }` dynamic object for runtime keys). A numeric-literal key still can't be declared in an `interface`/type annotation.
No duplicate-`__proto__`-key detection (Annex B legacy `SyntaxError` rule).

entries.name: Getters / setters on classes and object literals
entries.statusRow: Getters / setters (get x() {} / set x(v) {}) on classes and object literals
entries.description: get/set are contextual (not reserved). No new storage: an accessor is registered as an ordinary method under an internal dispatch key. obj.x / obj.x = v / compound assignment all route through the accessor, including from inside the class's own methods and through optional chaining. On object literals too: the literal is lowered to a synthetic anonymous class so the accessor body gets a real this reading/writing the object's own fields.
differences: An accessor-bearing object literal can't be assigned to a differently-shaped structural object type (its accessors are methods, not fields) — a clean rejection; used directly it works.
console.log of an accessor object prints only its data fields, not x: [Getter].
Static accessors, and logical assignment (`&&=`/`||=`/`??=`) on an accessor, remain out of scope for V1.

entries.name: new Error(msg)
entries.description: The base Error constructor.

entries.name: Built-in Error subtypes
entries.statusRow: Built-in Error subtypes (new TypeError(msg), RangeError, SyntaxError, EvalError, URIError, ReferenceError, DOMException) and instanceof against them
entries.description: A small fixed kind enum (a hidden runtime tag on the shared Error object shape, not a real class hierarchy), plus a real .name field. instanceof Error matches any kind; instanceof TypeError matches only that one. new DOMException(message?, name?) takes its .name from the 2nd argument.
differences: `class X extends Error` works one level deep — construction, `super(msg)`, `.message`/`.name`, extra fields/methods, throw/catch with `instanceof` discrimination against sibling subclasses. Extending an Error *subclass* is a clean rejection, and `.stack`/`Error.captureStackTrace` don't exist.
`DOMException` carries no legacy numeric `.code`.

entries.name: new Array<T>(n)
entries.description: Constructs an array of length n.

entries.name: new Map<K,V>()
entries.description: Constructs a Map.

entries.name: new Set<T>()
entries.description: Constructs a Set.

entries.name: class (fields, constructor, methods, this, new)
entries.statusRow: class (fields, constructor, methods, this, new ClassName(args))
entries.signature: class C { x: number; constructor(x) { this.x = x } m() {} }
entries.description: Instances reuse the same heap-object/GEP machinery interfaces use; methods compile to plain static calls (this as an implicit first arg). Instance-field initializers work, and a class with fields needs no explicit constructor. Static field initializers run in declaration order. Qualified constructors/bases parse.
differences: A **derived** class adding fields when its base has a rest-parameter constructor requires an explicit `super(...)`. An instance-field initializer lowered into the constructor can currently see the constructor's own parameters (which real JS's separate initializer scope forbids), and an unannotated initializer of an unrecognized expression shape falls back to `i64`.
A computed/dynamic member name is a clean rejection; the recognized well-known-symbol keys are `[Symbol.asyncIterator]` and `[Symbol.iterator]`.
A class expression used as a runtime value or a named self-reference (`class D {...}` whose body references `D`) is a clean rejection; `extends <expression>` is out of scope.

Class early-error gaps (deferred): a field initializer containing `arguments` or a `super()` call, a `super()` in a method parameter default, field-definition ASI on the same line, and the `#constructor` private-name ban all compile instead of raising the spec's `SyntaxError`.

The **`readonly` field modifier** is enforced as a compile-time immutability check — a write is allowed only in the declaring class's constructor and rejected elsewhere (method, outside `obj.x = v`, nested closure, subclass constructor). Deep immutability (`readonly xs: number[]` then `xs.push(...)`) stays unenforced, matching TS.

entries.name: Constructor parameter properties
entries.statusRow: Constructor parameter properties (constructor(public x: number, readonly y: T))
entries.signature: class C { constructor(public x: number, private readonly y: string) {} }
entries.description: A visibility/readonly modifier on a constructor parameter (public/private/protected/readonly) both declares the field and assigns it from the parameter — the TypeScript shorthand for the declare-plus-assign boilerplate.
differences: Desugars at parse time to a declared field plus a `this.x = x` constructor prologue; `private`/`protected` get the same enforcement as ordinary declared fields, and `readonly` is enforced (a write after construction is rejected).
The modifiers are valid only on a constructor parameter — elsewhere they are a clean parse error.

entries.name: class static members / visibility / abstract / implements
entries.statusRow: class static members/static {} blocks, private/protected visibility, abstract classes/methods, implements
entries.signature: class C { static x = 1; static {} private y; abstract m(); }
entries.description: static members are inherited through extends (a non-redeclared static field shares its base's storage). private/protected are compile-time-only (zero runtime check, matching TS erasure) and reject super.privateMethod(). abstract reuses override-detection; implements is a compile-time structural self-check.

entries.name: Real JS/TS #x runtime-private field syntax
entries.description: Fields, methods, static fields/methods, and get/set accessors — exact-class-only access (the same rule private enforces), plus real reflection-hiding (Object.keys/.values/.entries/JSON.stringify/spread never see a #-named field, unlike private's type-level-only erasure).
differences: No class-field-initializer syntax (`#x = 1;` — a pre-existing gap for every field, not `#`-specific).
No early-error check for a `#m`/`static #m` name collision in the same class, or for the `#constructor`-is-always-banned rule.

entries.name: class inheritance (extends/super)
entries.signature: class D extends B { constructor() { super(); } }
entries.description: Single inheritance, base-first field layout, super(args)/super.method(args), and an implicit pass-through constructor when a derived class adds no fields. Dispatch is static except for a method provably overridden somewhere, which goes through a per-tree vtable (decided at compile time via whole-program analysis). extends also accepts EventEmitter<T>.

entries.name: instanceof (against user-defined classes)
entries.description: Every instance carries a hidden runtime type tag. A class-typed variable whose static class is T or an ancestor of T folds to a compile-time constant; one whose static class is an ancestor of the right-hand class needs a real runtime tag read. instanceof against Array/Map/Set/Date/RegExp is a compile-time constant.
differences: `x instanceof Object` is a compile-time constant — true for any non-primitive (class instance, object, array, function, Date, Map/Set, RegExp, …), false for a primitive. Only an undecidable static type (any/union/nullable) is a clean rejection.

entries.name: Experimental decorators — class, property, parameter & method @decorator
entries.statusRow: Experimental decorators — class, property, parameter & method @decorator
entries.description: Experimental class (constructor), property (target, key), parameter (target, key, index), and method (target, key, descriptor) decorators run at the class's source position — member decorators first, then class decorators (bottom-up). A method decorator receives a live descriptor whose value is the method as a callable; mutating descriptor.value or returning a new descriptor re-routes that method's calls through a per-method runtime slot. With -emit-decorator-metadata, decorated members and a decorated class's constructor get design:* metadata readable via Reflect.getMetadata.
differences: A class decorator that returns a replacement constructor is refused at runtime (a loud throw) — the static-class model has no constructor-replacement routing yet; observe-only class decorators (registration) run faithfully. A generic class decorator is a compile-time rejection.

Accessor (get/set), static, and generator method decorators, and method decorators on a generic class, are rejected; so is a method whose parameter/return types can't be marshalled (array/nullable/rest params).

Factory-call decorators (@dec(...) — the @Controller('/api')/@Get('/users') shape) work across placements, including a returned closure that captures the factory's arguments (dynamic functions now carry their captures). The standard dialect covers every member placement — class, method, instance-field, getter/setter, and accessor auto-field decorators — plus context.addInitializer (per-instance). A decorated `accessor x` desugars to a backing field + get/set and follows the TC39 { get, set, init } protocol. A decorator that *replaces* a method/getter/setter can't do typed this.field access (the replacement runs with a boxed this) — observe-only and init decorators are unaffected.

The standard (TC39) (value, context) dialect (-decorators=standard, default is experimental) runs class and method decorators; its field/accessor/getter-setter decorators and context.addInitializer are a rejected sub-stage, and TC39 has no parameter decorators. design:* metadata types are name-carrying descriptors, not the real constructors.
